keySentence: Growing up means leaving Neverland — but you carry its magic inside forever.

facts.Page story text 1 (draft, teacher check: One night Peter Pan came back to the window just as Wendy had always secretly hoped he someday might. But it was not Wendy who heard him this time — it was her daughter Jane who was sitting up waiting. Wendy watched from across the darkened room as Jane flew away into the starlit London sky after him. She felt a small and unexpected ache that she had not quite prepared herself to feel that quiet night. But alongside the ache she also felt something warm — a gratitude for having flown when she had the chance. She understood at last that Neverland is not a place you stay but a place you carry away inside you always. Growing up means leaving Neverland — but you carry its magic inside forever.
facts.Page story text 2 (draft, teacher check: Watching her daughter Jane fly away with Peter Pan, Wendy felt two things simultaneously and completely. She felt loss — the reminder that her own Neverland was gone and could not be returned to or reclaimed. And she felt something else — a deep satisfaction that the magic had not ended with her but had continued past her. She had passed Neverland to Jane not through fairy dust but through the stories she had told every single night. Those stories had kept the window open, had kept the possibility alive, had made Jane ready for Peter when he came. Wendy understood that this was the most important thing she had ever done and perhaps the most Neverland thing of all. She had grown up and left the island and somehow managed to bring the essential part of it with her and pass it on. Growing up means leaving Neverland — but you carry its magic inside forever.
facts.Page story text 3 (draft, teacher check: The final image of Wendy watching Jane fly away is Barrie's most complex and quietly devastating piece of writing. It captures with perfect economy what it feels like to understand something fully only after the opportunity has passed. Wendy sees clearly now what she could only half-see during her own time in Neverland — what it was and what it meant. But clarity, as it often does, arrives precisely at the moment when it can inform memory rather than current experience. This is not presented as tragedy, however, but as the natural and even beautiful rhythm of how magic moves through time. It passes from person to person through stories, not through the original experience being somehow magically preserved. Wendy is the link between her own Neverland and Jane's — the carrier of the magic across the gap of her own growing up. She could not stay in Neverland but she kept it alive, which turns out to be something more lasting and more generous. Growing up means leaving Neverland — but you carry its magic inside forever.
